transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been troubling you or what brings you in today?

Hi, yeah, thanks. Well, the main thing, and honestly it’s been driving me absolutely crazy lately because I’m 26 now and I really need to get things together, is that I get pulled off track by just... every single little sound or thought. 

Like, for example, I’ve been trying to work on this job application. I really need to get it done because I need work, obviously, since I've just been sitting around. So I sit down, I get everything ready, I tell myself I'm going to focus, but then, I swear, a car will drive by outside. Not even a loud car, just tires on the pavement, and I have to look out the window to see what it is. Or my phone screen will light up for a split second because of some junk email, and suddenly I'm holding my phone. Or even just my own brain—like some totally random idea pops into my head about what I should make for lunch, or I start wondering how they film those deep-sea nature documentaries, and it just sends me somewhere completely else. 

And the crazy part is, I don't even notice it happening. I'll be forty-five minutes deep into reading articles about submarines before I realize I was supposed to be typing in my high school graduation year on the application. It just pulls me away before I even have a chance to stop it, and it's so frustrating because I really do want to just finish the form, but it's like every tiny thing in the room or in my head is demanding my attention all at once and I just follow it without even thinking.

When you think about these difficulties with staying focused and getting pulled off track, did you notice these same kinds of problems when you were a child, like in school or doing homework, or is this something that started more recently as an adult?

Oh, man, no, this is definitely not new. It’s... it’s always been like this. I mean, if I really think back on it, even when I was super young, like, in elementary school, it was the exact same story, just in a different setting, you know? 

Like, I remember my teachers—Mrs. Gable in third grade, Mr. Henderson in fourth, they all did it—they were constantly, and I mean constantly, moving my desk. They’d put me right up front by their desk, or sometimes they’d stick me in the back corner by myself because I just could not stop talking. I’d just blurt things out, completely out of turn, because a thought would pop into my head and it felt like I had to say it right that second before it disappeared, even if someone else was talking or the teacher was in the middle of a lesson. 

And homework? Oh, forget about it. I’d either forget to write down what the assignment was, or I’d write it down but leave the book at school, or I’d actually do the homework and then leave it sitting on the kitchen counter the next morning. My mom used to get so mad because she’d spend all this time helping me do it, and then I’d just leave it at home. 

And when I did do the work in class, like those math worksheets where you had to do fifty addition problems in two minutes or whatever, I’d just rush through them. I just wanted to be done so I could go do something else, anything else. So I’d make all these stupid, careless mistakes. I’d add instead of subtract, or I’d skip whole rows of questions without even realizing it. I knew how to do the math, but my brain was just going a million miles an hour and I couldn't slow down enough to actually pay attention to what my pencil was doing. So, yeah, it’s definitely not a new adult thing, it’s just... it’s always been my normal, I guess, which is why it’s so frustrating that I still haven’t figured out how to fix it.
